Weariness
WEER-ee-nes
n.
From weary + -ness; weary from Old English wērig, “tired, exhausted.” Renders the Hebrew yāga, “to be weary, work hard,” and the Greek kopos, “labor to weariness,” and ekluō, “to faint, grow weary.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Weariness in Scripture is the real, often-honored, sometimes-warned-against fatigue of soul or body that comes from sustained labor, prolonged suffering, hard providences, persistent sin, or the long discouragement of waiting. The Bible does not pretend the saint will be exempt; it teaches him both how to bear the weariness rightly and how to recover from it. Christ Himself, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well at Sychar; the Christ in whom dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily was a man who could be tired by the road. Paul is candid about his ministerial weariness: in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. The prophets weary themselves in pleading; the saints weary themselves in waiting; the soul wearies itself in sin (thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way, says the LORD to apostate Israel); the body wearies under the sun, the curse, and the years. Against all weariness Scripture presses promises and disciplines. The promise to those who wait: but they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint. The promise to those who labor in the gospel: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. The promise to those who endure: consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. The Christ who came down from heaven to make atonement makes also the offer to the weary themselves: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Weariness is therefore real, honored when borne in the Lord’s work, warned against when it tempts toward faintness in well-doing, and answered by the rest Christ offers—a rest that is not the absence of all labor but the deeper rest of the soul taking its load upon Him and finding His yoke easy and His burden light.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WEARINESS as the state of being weary; lassitude or exhaustion of strength or feeling, induced by labor; fatigue; tedium; in scripture, the real fatigue of soul or body that meets the saint in the Lord’s service and waits to be answered by His promised rest.

expand to see more

WEARINESS, n. — 1. The state of being weary; that lassitude or exhaustion of strength which is induced by labor; fatigue; tedium. 2. The state of being affected with feelings of disgust at being detained too long. 3. In scripture, the real fatigue of soul or body that comes from sustained labor, prolonged suffering, or hard providence—to be borne in the Lord’s strength and answered by the rest Christ offers.

WEARY, a. — 1. Having the strength exhausted by toil or exertion; tired; fatigued. 2. Having the patience exhausted, or the mind yielding to discouragement.

📖 Key Scripture

Isaiah 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Galatians 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Matthew 11:28-29 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

John 4:6 — "Now Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Weariness is corrupted, on one side, by the comfort-and-self-care register of the present age that treats every weariness as a problem to be eliminated rather than a real fatigue to be borne in the Lord and answered by His rest—and on the other by the flesh-driven workaholism that despises weariness as weakness and ignores Christ’s own invitation to the weary.

expand to see more

The comfort-and-self-care register of the present age treats every weariness as a problem to be eliminated by better boundaries, more self-care, and reduced commitment. Scripture acknowledges weariness as a real fatigue of soul and body, sometimes honored (Paul’s ministerial weariness), sometimes warned against (the temptation to faint in well-doing), and always to be borne in the Lord’s strength and answered by the promised rest. The reflexive contemporary instinct to reduce commitments at the first sign of fatigue can produce a Christianity that has never strained itself in the Lord’s service and so has never had the occasion to prove the strength He promises to those who wait on Him. The biblical disposition is different: when the weariness comes, it is borne, brought to the Lord, set against the eschatological harvest (in due season we shall reap, if we faint not), and answered by the rest of the One who Himself was wearied on the way and who promises rest to all who come to Him with their load.

The opposite corruption is the flesh-driven workaholism that despises weariness as weakness and ignores Christ’s own invitation to the weary. The minister or saint who treats fatigue as failure, who refuses to come to the Lord with his load, who runs in his own strength without ever taking up the easy yoke and the light burden, eventually finds either burnout or embittered exhaustion at the end of his striving. Christ’s invitation is not optional. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. The weary saint is to come; the weary minister is to come; the load is to be brought to the One who has invited the bringing; the yoke is to be exchanged for the easier one; and the rest is to be received not as the absence of all labor but as the deeper rest of the soul resting in the strength of its Lord. Recover both ends: refuse the comfort culture’s premature retreat from sustained service, and refuse the flesh-driven workaholism that scorns the weariness Christ invites the weary to bring.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yāga (to be weary, work hard) and lā’āh (to be weary); Greek kopos (labor to weariness) and ekluō (to faint, grow weary)—the real fatigue of soul or body, borne in the Lord and answered by His promised rest.

expand to see more

Hebrew yāga (H3021) — to be weary, work hard.

Hebrew lā’āh (H3811) — to be weary, exhausted (Isa 1:14; Jer 6:11).

Greek kopos (G2873) — labor, toil, weariness (2 Cor 11:27).

Greek ekluō (G1590) — to be loosed out, faint, grow weary (Gal 6:9; Heb 12:3, 5).

Usage

"They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength... they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint—the promise to those who wait."

"Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not—the warning to those who serve."

"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest—Christ’s invitation to the weary themselves."
